sourceInformation.genre: Third-person action-horror shooter with crowd control, resource management and an escort
sourceInformation.perspective: Over-the-shoulder third person with a laser sight; letterboxed cinematic cameras; one on-rails shooting finale
sourceInformation.tech: Riftlight pixel-engine 0.46.0 (three.js r186 WebGPU, Rapier), plain JavaScript modules bundled with esbuild, AI Hub session client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine native pixel style at 480 by 270 with a soft vignette: palette toon materials, data-driven puppets and props, plus library props for generic things
sourceInformation.animation: Engine clip system on the hero rig: masked upper and lower layers, about 60 new clips and gaits, spring-chain scarf, ragdolls, head look
sourceInformation.audio: All code, no files. Ten original songs as data with music at 10 percent by default, about 60 synthesised sound effects, Animalese-style gibberish voices per speaker
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol v1 shared-world co-op (1 to 4); standalone parties over BroadcastChannel and WebRTC invite codes with a public STUN server
sourceInformation.testing: Headless node scripts and Playwright browsers on this computer, behind one command (node tools/test.mjs): a scripted whole-game playthrough, unit and AI suites, stubbed gamepad, phone profile, Web Audio levels, two-page parties, the AI Hub harness. The game itself, the AI Hub harness and a stubbed touch-only device also ran in Firefox with WebGPU forced on, a virtual display and a null audio sink. WebKit has no WebGPU here, so it shows the clear message. No subagents for review. No human playtest.
sourceInformation.research: Read the design plan, the engine kit guide, API and assets docs, and the AI Hub protocol README and example. No web research on the source.

testingFeedback: 52, itemised in docs/TESTING.md: 21 from the whole-game bot playthrough, 9 from the node suites, 11 from browser and harness runs, 10 from captures, 1 from checking the code against the plan. Bugs in the bot or the tests themselves are not counted, and how to split or merge an issue is a judgement call.

15. For example: reloading a checkpoint left the game stuck; set pieces changed shared level data and broke every retry; a mid-vault checkpoint put you inside a wall; the road had no door action; the final boss could not be hurt; launch mines could not be shot; Night Shift crashed on its first frame; opening the Case with Triangle dropped your gun; Esc opened Pause and shut it in the same frame; hub traffic starved under slow rendering, and a host leaving early could fail the hub check.
The scripted whole-game playthrough in Node. It runs about 60 times faster than real time, so one run of the entire game took under a minute, and it found most of the game-breaking bugs.
The per-sound render checks. They stayed green after the first run. They guard against typos, but never found a gameplay problem.
engineFeedback: Engine.headless. The same game code runs in Node with no GPU, deterministic and very fast, so a bot can play the whole game. A close second is writing models, textures and clips as plain data.

A few times. One model id clashed with the library (armchair) and the catalog threw. shelf is not an id, it is bookshelf. TEXTURE_LIBRARY.get throws rather than returning null. I also wrongly blamed dropped pad presses at time scale 0 for a menu bug that was my own; a direct test showed pad presses work there. And I wrongly concluded the game could not run in Firefox here, because my first attempt had no display. A full-size ground collider silently blocked shots at things below y = 0.

The Intent layer with the shared Bot and the story stage system. Everything else, from attract mode to the playthrough test, hangs off them. After that, the over-the-shoulder aiming with hit zones built from joint positions.
Working out frame and input timing at low frame rates in the software WebGPU browser here: which presses survive, when a level swap really happens, and what can run at time scale 0.
An official shoulder-offset third-person rig, so a game need not replace rig.step by hand.
promptFeedback: The plan is a complete design with verified engine facts, real numbers and a real script. I could spend the effort on building instead of guessing. The originality guardrails were clear too.

Mostly the Online line, which is only a link, until the plan explained it. The plan also lists more animations and props than a single vertical slice strictly needs, so I had to judge where a shared clip was good enough.

Keeping every system working together across a long linear game alone: the Dame, the crowd AI, checkpoints and set pieces all interact, and most of the serious bugs were at those joins. I could not judge game feel with hands on a pad here, only through the bot and screenshots.

Ask for a short human-style feel checklist that a script can approximate, and say up front which listed assets are required and which are optional. A real person should still play it: balance here was only tuned against the bot.

aiHub.name: PRESIDENT EVIL 4
aiHub.description: An insurance adjuster goes alone to a storm-beaten island to recover the rudest woman alive. Over-the-shoulder precision shooting, kicks, a sample case, a merchant in a diving helmet, and a villain on the loudspeakers.
aiHub.controls: Pad: L2 aim, R2 fire, Cross kick and action, Circle run. Keyboard and mouse: WASD, right mouse aim, left mouse fire, E action, Shift run.
